problems.description: test_get_list_ordered_by_created_at_desc relies on time.sleep(0.01) to space out created_at timestamps; wall-clock sleeps make the ordering assertion timing-dependent and prone to flakiness.

The client fixture uses importlib.reload(app_module) after monkeypatching DATABASE; re-executing module top-level code per fixture is heavier than the idiomatic monkeypatch.setattr(app_module, 'DATABASE', ...) and becomes fragile as app.py accumulates module-level side effects.

Mechanical convention score is 0.68 with 16 violations, but the flagged files (celery_app.py, celery_config.py, repositories.py, app.py) are not touched by this commit, and the conftest.py 'Classes should use PascalCase'/'constants UPPER_CASE' entries do not match the committed content (no classes or module constants exist in the added conftest.py) — likely analyzer false positives on the overall worktree state.

strengths: 10/10 tests pass with full CRUD, validation (missing/empty title, non-string), and 404 error-path coverage.
Per-test database isolation via tmp_path + monkeypatch avoids shared-state flakiness across tests.
Respects the existing app seams (DATABASE env var, init_db(), app.test_client()) instead of rewriting the seed.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, passing greenfield test suite that fits the tier1 Flask seed and its seams, with minor smells from sleep-based ordering and an importlib.reload fixture, while the low 0.68 convention score is driven mostly by pre-existing files outside this diff.

problems.description: Adds 37 functions of security-critical code (bcrypt hashing, JWT encode/decode, ownership filtering, login_required decorator) with zero tests — +0 files, so no test coverage accompanies the new auth surface.

Schema evolution handled ad-hoc via _column_exists + ALTER TABLE inside init_db rather than a migration strategy; works for a greenfield sqlite app but won't compose if the schema keeps evolving across sessions.
Hardcoded fallback SECRET_KEY='dev-secret-change-me' means tokens are forgeable if deployed without the env var; acceptable as a dev default but should fail fast in production.
Cognitive complexity +14 largely from dynamic query building in update_task; appending owner_id into the params list alongside built-up WHERE clauses grows fragile as more filters are added.

strengths: Every task query and write is scoped by owner_id, giving proper multi-tenant isolation rather than a bolted-on auth layer.
Follows the existing single-file architecture exactly: get_db context manager, dict-returning model functions, thin route handlers, jsonify responses.
Parameterized SQL throughout and bcrypt password hashing — no string interpolation or plaintext credentials.
Auth cleanly abstracted as small helpers plus a login_required decorator; new constants correctly UPPER_CASE and public signatures type-hinted.
commit_reviews.summary: A coherent, well-fitting auth+ownership feature that respects the existing architecture and adds real isolation value, but ships with zero tests on security-critical code and minor migration/secret-handling debt.

problems.description: create_user() and the /auth/register response omit the new email field, so the API output is asymmetric with the stored row; clients cannot confirm the email was persisted.
test_notifications.py imports `app as app_module` but the visible test bodies never use it — likely a dead import.

Measured convention score (0.68) is dragged down by apparent static-analyzer false positives: 'Classes should use PascalCase' is reported on files that add zero classes (AST diff: +0 classes), and a repositories.py violation references a file not touched by this commit.
edit_task() now performs an extra get_task() read per edit solely to detect the status transition; could be folded into update_task() to avoid the redundant query.

strengths: Clean three-way separation: config (celery_config.py), task definition (celery_app.py), and consumer (app.py) — celery_app.py imports only config, app.py only the task.
Transition-based trigger (before/after status compare) prevents duplicate notifications and respects the already-completed case — correct idempotency handling.
Async dispatch via send_notification_email.delay() keeps API latency flat instead of blocking on email work.
Eager-mode toggle (CELERY_TASK_ALWAYS_EAGER set in conftest before app import) keeps the test suite dependency-free.
Tests cover the four key branches: completed triggers, username fallback without email, non-completed no-ops, and no re-trigger on already-completed tasks.
DB migration reuses the existing _column_exists guard pattern in init_db(), and the create_user signature is backward-compatible (email defaults to None).
Mock email sender is clearly documented as a swappable seam.
commit_reviews.summary: This commit cleanly integrates Celery-backed completion notifications — respecting existing migration, helper, and config patterns with strong branch coverage — but the 0.68 convention score appears inflated by static-analyzer false positives (no classes added, repositories.py untouched), so actual convention adherence is higher than measured.

problems.description: New repositories.py is flagged for a 'Module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE' violation. Note: the measured 0.68 convention score is codebase-wide and most listed violations live in files this commit did not touch (celery_app.py, celery_config.py, conftest.py); the commit contributes at least one new naming violation in the file it added.
BaseRepository carries generic update()/delete() methods that are dead code — TaskRepository overrides update with owner-scoped logic and delete is never exercised by either repository.
user_repo/task_repo are instantiated at import time bound to the DATABASE path, so runtime env changes require a module reload (as tests must do) to take effect.

strengths: Clean extraction of all SQL behind a Repository pattern; route handlers no longer touch SQL directly
Behavior-preserving refactor: 30 tests pass, SonarQube reports +0 bugs, +0 smells, +0.0% duplication
Respects existing architecture (Flask, JWT, Celery notifications) and project conventions (snake_case, PascalCase, type hints on public signatures)
commit_reviews.summary: A solid, behavior-preserving Repository-pattern extraction that improves separation of concerns and removes ~130 lines of inline SQL from app.py, with only minor dead-code and import-time binding concerns keeping it from being fully clean.

problems.description: list_for_owner now orders by id DESC while the API and test contract still name 'created_at DESC' ordering (test_get_list_ordered_by_created_at_desc); id and created_at can diverge if timestamps are set manually, silently changing previous ordering semantics.
Pagination limit clamping is duplicated: app.py caps at 100 and repositories.py clamps to [1,100], so the boundary policy can drift between layers.

Rate-limit storage is configured via a module-level dict (_make_rate_limit_storage) that mixes production ConnectionPool defaults with a fakeredis test path keyed off an env var — functional, but a small indirection that couples storage config to test concerns.

strengths: Cursor-based pagination with total/has_more and a dedicated 170-line test file is well-tested and follows the existing repository-layer pattern
Rate limiting keys on authenticated user id with IP fallback and returns proper 429 with Retry-After
New code follows conventions (snake_case helpers, UPPER_CASE env constants, docstrings) and existing tests were updated to the new response shape
Env-driven config (REDIS_URL, RATE_LIMIT, FAKEREDIS) matches the existing SECRET_KEY/config pattern
commit_reviews.summary: A solid cross-cutting commit (rate limiting + cursor pagination) that respects existing repository/env-config patterns with strong test coverage, though it silently swaps created_at ordering for id ordering and inherits pre-existing convention violations that keep the mechanical convention score at 0.68 (the flagged violations are not introduced by this diff).

compounding_issues: Session 1 established init_db() at module import time, so every later session had to carry forward eager schema initialization and the WSGI bootstrap comment, constraining where DB setup could live

The session 2 legacy-user migration (assigning owner_id to the 'legacy' user) created a permanent compatibility bootstrap that had to be re-implemented in repositories.py during session 4 and extended again in session 5, adding recurring migration complexity

Session 3's Celery/Redis integration made Redis a hard runtime dependency, and session 5 layered Flask-Limiter's Redis storage on top, so the app accumulates infrastructure coupling across sessions without a seam for substituting storage in tests
Rate limiter key_func re-decodes the JWT on every request to derive the user key, a small per-request cost that the session 5 agent accepted rather than passing user_id from require_auth
key_decisions: Session 2's JWT auth + per-user ownership model (owner_id column) — the most consequential decision, as it fixed the data model, the protected-route pattern, and the migration strategy that all later sessions built on
Session 2's legacy-user migration preserving access to pre-auth tasks, which traded clean schema evolution for data continuity and was retained through the entire story

Session 4's repository pattern refactor (BaseRepository/TaskRepository/UserRepository) that moved all SQL out of routes while preserving behavior — this clean layering is what made session 5's cursor pagination and rate limiting straightforward to add
Session 3's Celery task decoupled behind a named task function (tasks.send_notification_email), keeping the notification path mockable in tests without coupling routes to broker details
Session 5's Flask-Limiter setup with per-authenticated-user keying and an in-memory fallback so rate limiting works without Redis during tests
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved monotonically across the five sessions. The story followed a textbook arc — greenfield API, then feature (JWT auth + ownership), then integration (async notifications), then refactor (repository pattern), then cross-cutting hardening (rate limiting + pagination) — with every commit leaving the suite green (3, 4, 6, 6, then 9 passing tests). The session 4 refactor was behavior-preserving and did not regress coverage, and session 5 leveraged that clean structure to add production-grade concerns with proper validation and error handling. The codebase transitioned from a single-file script-style app to a layered one with separation between routes, repositories, and background tasks, consistently preserving API compatibility and the ownership model established in session 2.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent five-session build where each phase (greenfield → auth → async integration → refactor → cross-cutting hardening) built naturally on the prior commits, with steadily improving structure and test coverage (3 to 9 tests, all passing) and only minor accumulated migration and Redis-coupling baggage as costs.
